facts.body: This album became the accidental home of the first hidden track, "Her Majesty". The track was initially intended to be removed from the final cut by Paul McCartney, but due to Abbey Road Studios' policy of leaving edited material at the end of the master tape and a subsequent oversight by the mastering engineer, it was inadvertently included after 20 seconds of silence, a surprise the band ultimately decided to keep. "When the Beatles reviewed the master and were surprised by that song coming out of the silence, they thought it was really cool. Leave it in, they said. facts.title: Montreal Bed-In for Peace (1969)
facts.body: Yoko Ono and John Lennon held their famous "bed-in" in room 1742 at the Fairmont Queen Elizabeth hotel in Montreal in 1969, as a protest against war and a call for peace. "That's where John and Yoko held their famous bed in back in 1969."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Yoko Ono

facts.title: Montreal Bed-In for Peace (1969)
facts.body: Yoko Ono and her partner John Lennon held a week-long non-violent "bed-in for peace" protest in Montreal from May 26 to June 1, 1969, as a novel form of activism against the Vietnam War. This event was a successor to their Amsterdam bed-in and was relocated to Montreal after Lennon was denied entry to the US and a brief, uncomfortable stay in the Bahamas. "On May 26th, June 1st, 1969, he held a bed in for peace protest in Montreal."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Yoko Ono

facts.title: Queen Elizabeth Hotel Stay (1969)
facts.body: Yoko Ono and John Lennon arrived in Montreal on May 26, 1969, and resided in rooms 1738, 1740, 1742, and 1744 at the Queen Elizabeth Hotel for their bed-in. This location was chosen for its proximity to New York, aiding American press coverage. "John and Yoko flew to Montreal on May 26th and stayed in the room 1738, 1740, 1742, and 1744 at the Queen Elizabeth Hotel."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Yoko Ono

facts.title: Notable Visitors During Bed-In (1969)
facts.body: During their Montreal bed-in, Yoko Ono and John Lennon were visited by prominent figures such as Timothy Leary, Tommy Smothers, Dick Gregory, Murray the K, Al Capp, Alan Ginsburg, and then-Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau. "During the week in Montreal, the couple was visited by Timothy Leary, Tommy Smothers, Dick Gregory, Murray the Kay, Al Cap, Alan Ginsburg, and of course, Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Yoko Ono

facts.body: On a 1969 episode of "The Glenn Campbell Goodtime Hour," Campbell performed a soulful rendition of Bob Dylan's "Blowin' in the Wind" with Stevie Wonder, a pairing he later cited as one of the highlights of his show. facts.title: The Glenn Campbell Goodtime Hour (1969-1971)
facts.body: Debuting on January 29, 1969, this show replaced the canceled Smothers Brothers Show. While it featured some comedy that hasn't aged well, its music was its distinguishing factor. The show, with Nelson Riddle as music director, showcased Campbell's country-pop blend and hosted a wide array of artists from various genres. It was eventually canceled in 1971 after four seasons, despite its success, surviving the "rural purge" for about a year. "The show did well enough that the Glenn Campbell Good Time Arrow was born debuting on January 29, 1969 and you guessed it, it became the replacement for the canceled Smothers Brothers Show."

facts.body: This album was produced by John Cale of The Velvet Underground. Due to the band's inability to rehearse for more than 20 minutes, half the material was allegedly written the night before their first day in the studio, with old avant-garde ideas reworked into more coherent songs. facts.title: The Glenn Campbell Goodtime Hour (1969-1971)
facts.body: Debuting on January 29, 1969, this show replaced the canceled Smothers Brothers Show. While it featured some comedy that hasn't aged well, its music was its distinguishing factor. The show, with Nelson Riddle as music director, showcased Campbell's country-pop blend and hosted a wide array of artists from various genres. It was eventually canceled in 1971 after four seasons, despite its success, surviving the "rural purge" for about a year. "The show did well enough that the Glenn Campbell Good Time Arrow was born debuting on January 29, 1969 and you guessed it, it became the replacement for the canceled Smothers Brothers Show."

facts.body: Released in May 1969, this double album was two years in the making and revolves around the character Tommy Walker. *Rolling Stone*'s 1969 review summarized its plot: Tommy becomes blind, deaf, and dumb after witnessing a murder, eventually becoming a pinball champion, reaching a state of grace, regaining his senses, starting a religion, and finally being discarded by his disciples and returning to isolation. Roger Daltrey later reflected that the album served as a "spiritual awakening" for American youth grappling with the Vietnam War and conscription, deeply capturing people's imaginations. "The opera is, apart from being some of the best rock yet, a statement of Townsend's philosophy. It's about life, he says."

facts.body: Brainstormed after watching Stanley Kubrick's "2001: A Space Odyssey," this song tells the story of Major Tom, an isolated astronaut. It captured the 1969 zeitgeist, was rushed by Mercury Records for the Apollo 11 moon landing, and became a UK number five hit. In 1973, it belatedly became Bowie's first US Top 40 hit, peaking at number 15/16 on the Hot 100, years after its initial release. "He called the song Space Odyssey and it would change everything, ushering Bowie into his next phase."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.name: Space Oddity

facts.body: Emerging after Bowie saw Stanley Kubrick's "2001: Space Odyssey" while stoned in 1968, this song was inspired by the film's character David Bowman and possibly Tom Major, a failed British trapeze artist who also made garden gnomes. Initially rejected multiple times as a "novelty song," it became Bowie's first hit due to the BBC using it as a theme for their Apollo Moon mission coverage. It reached number five on the UK charts, but only peaked at number 124 in North America initially, before a 1973 re-release saw it reach number 15 in the US and number 16 in Canada. "That song became David Bowie's first ever hit. And only because of some lucky timing."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Space Oddity

facts.body: The original studio recording of "Space Oddity" in 1969 was a psychedelic folk rocker about Major Tom, which Bowie re-recorded later that year after signing a new record deal. It debuted in Billboard in August 1969 and bubbled under the Hot 100, peaking at number 124. In early 1973, four years after its recording, RCA Records re-issued the song on 45, pushing it to American Top 40 radio with new Ziggy Stardust imagery. It finally made the Hot 100, peaking at number 15, solidifying Bowie's alien persona and defining him in the public imagination. "In early 1973, four years after it had been recorded, Space Audity finally made the Hot 100, peaking at number 15."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.name: Space Oddity

facts.body: This dark, pseudo-folk song was written by Bowie in the context of a painful breakup with Hermione Farthingdale, feelings of depression, and a fascination with the American space program, particularly the Apollo moon landing and the film *2001, A Space Odyssey*. The very first version was recorded on February 2nd, 1969, the day after his breakup. Several more versions followed, with the definitive one recorded on June 20th and released on July 11th, just in time for the Apollo 11 mission. Broadcasters, including the BBC, adopted it as an unofficial theme for the July 20th moon landing. The song became Bowie's breakthrough hit and turned him into a star, though he feared becoming a one-hit wonder. Its lyrics about Major Tom sparked speculation about the character's identity. Bowie recorded the definitive version after a chance meeting with Elton John led him to a producer. "The definitive version was recorded June 20th, and then released to the public on July 11th, just in time for the Apollo 11 mission."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

The song became Bowie's breakthrough hit and turned him into a star, though he feared becoming a one-hit wonder. Its lyrics about Major Tom sparked speculation about the character's identity. Bowie recorded the definitive version after a chance meeting with Elton John led him to a producer. "The definitive version was recorded June 20th, and then released to the public on July 11th, just in time for the Apollo 11 mission."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Space Oddity

facts.body: This song emerged almost fully formed after Bowie saw Stanley Kubrick's "2001, A Space Odyssey" in 1968, with the character David Bowman potentially inspiring "Major Tom." It was initially rejected but then demoed for RCA Records. Its success was linked to the Apollo moon missions, with the BBC using it for their coverage of the Man Moon Landings. The song reached number five on the charts in the UK, but only number 124 in North America initially, before being re-released in 1973 and reaching number 15 in the US and number 16 in Canada. "That song became David Bowie's first ever hits."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Space Oddity

facts.title: Defining Second Chance Hit
facts.body: The original studio recording of "Space Oddity" in 1969 was a psychedelic folk rocker about Major Tom, which Bowie re-recorded later that year after signing a new record deal. It debuted in Billboard in August 1969 and bubbled under the Hot 100, peaking at number 124. In early 1973, four years after its recording, RCA Records re-issued the song on 45, pushing it to American Top 40 radio with new Ziggy Stardust imagery. It finally made the Hot 100, peaking at number 15, solidifying Bowie's alien persona and defining him in the public imagination. "In early 1973, four years after it had been recorded, Space Audity finally made the Hot 100, peaking at number 15."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.name: Space Oddity

facts.title: Major Tom's Journey
facts.body: Brainstormed after watching Stanley Kubrick's "2001: A Space Odyssey," this song tells the story of Major Tom, an isolated astronaut. It captured the 1969 zeitgeist, was rushed by Mercury Records for the Apollo 11 moon landing, and became a UK number five hit. In 1973, it belatedly became Bowie's first US Top 40 hit, peaking at number 15/16 on the Hot 100, years after its initial release. "He called the song Space Odyssey and it would change everything, ushering Bowie into his next phase."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.name: Space Oddity

facts.title: Critics' Favorite Album
facts.body: In a survey comparing public and critical music tastes, critics specifically mentioned Captain Beefheart's 1969 album, *Trout Mask Replica*, as one of their favorites, calling it "baffling." This album is known for its experimental and challenging nature, appealing to a critical audience. "The critics professed to love Nick Cave and the bad seeds, The Fall, and Captain B. Farts baffling 1969 album Trout Mass Grapelka."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 60 Mind-Blowing Facts About Music in 60 Minutes: 2017 Edition
facts.name: Trout Mask Replica

facts.body: Released in October 1969, this album by the sculptor-turned-musician was so unconventional that it immediately became an underground classic. Most listeners found its 28 songs "absolutely completely and undeniably un-listenable," yet many, including the future Johnny Rotten of the Sex Pistols, bought and played it specifically for its challenging nature. Even today, it remains a difficult listen but opened "new possibilities" for a few. "Most who heard this album, which is called Trout Mask Replica, found it to be absolutely completely and undeniably un-listenable."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Trout Mask Replica

facts.title: Magnum Opus
facts.body: Released in 1969, this double album, comprising 28 tracks, is widely regarded by critics as Captain Beefheart's finest work. It resonated with specific music fans who appreciated its experimental nature, including The Beatles, Johnny Lydon of the Sex Pistols, Matt Groening, and film director David Lynch, all drawn to its "out there" and disagreeable sound. "His magnum opus, the record that critics say is his best work, came out in 1969."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Discovery by William Duke Rayner (1969)
facts.body: In 1969, William Duke Rayner, a furniture store owner from Nashville with aspirations in music, discovered Martell. He heard her covering country songs at an Air Force Base in South Carolina and was impressed by the audience's reaction, convincing her to let him fund a demo and become her manager. "He liked the reaction that he heard from the audience when Linda was singing at a Air Force Base in South Carolina."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country
facts.name: Linda Martell

facts.title: Grand Ole Opry Debut (1969)
facts.body: Linda Martell was the first solo female black artist to perform at the Grand Ole Opry, playing there a total of 12 times. During her performances at the Ryman Auditorium, she would have seen the words "Confederate gallery" hanging in the balcony, a sign that remained until its removal in 2017. "She was the first solo female black artist to do so and in fact she would play there 12 times in total."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

facts.title: Acquisition of Ticketron Name and Renaming (1969)
facts.body: In July 1969, TRS acquired the "Ticketron" name from another defunct computer ticketing company and officially rebranded itself as Ticketron, solidifying its position in the emerging market. "TRS, meanwhile, bought the name Ticketron from another company that crashed in burn trying to use computers to sell tickets. And in July 1969, TRS officially became Ticketron."

facts.title: Legendary Cult Record
facts.body: Released in 1969, this album by The Shaggs is considered one of the great cult records of the last 50 years. It is described as "weird" and "hard to listen to," often guaranteed to clear a party. Despite its unusual qualities, Kurt Cobain ranked it as number five on his top 50 albums of all time. "The result was a record called Philosophy of the World... That is one of the great cult records from the last 50 years. It is weird, it is hard to listen to, and guaranteed to chase everybody out of a party at the end of the night."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

Despite being considered "not that good" by conventional standards, it earned legendary status and was praised for the sincerity and authenticity of its heartfelt performances. facts.body: This "sweet" song became a number one hit for a month in 1969 and remained in the top 20 by November 22nd, 1969, enjoying constant airplay on AM radio. Produced by Ron Dante, who also produced records for Barry Manilow, its innocent, bubblegum pop sound stood in stark contrast to more sexually charged songs like Led Zeppelin's "Whole Lotta Love" on the radio at the same time. "Sweet, sweet song, sugar sugar by the Archies actually by Ron Dante who produced some of the Barry Manolo records that would come later in the 70s."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

facts.body: This song was the Billboard year-end number one for 1969, by "The Archies," who were fictional comic book characters from CBS's "The Archie Show." The band itself was composed of real-life session musicians created to promote the cartoon. It became a massive hit, topping the Hot 100 for four weeks and selling 3 million copies in 1969 alone, with these sales helping it secure the year-end title over strong contenders. "The Archies, The Band, made up of real-life session musicians, was created to promote the TV cartoon, and Sugar Sugar was a real and massive hit."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Hits of the Year Edition Part 2
facts.name: Sugar, Sugar

facts.body: This song, co-written by Jeff Barry and Andy Kim, was rejected by The Monkees, leading Don Kirshner to create The Archies as a fictional band to record it. Tony Dante sang all vocal parts, with his voice multi-tracked to create the illusion of a full band. Released around Memorial Day 1969, it initially struggled for radio play until Kirshner convinced a DJ in Texas to spin it, leading to a surge of requests. The song rapidly climbed the Billboard Hot 100, reaching number 41 in early August, then 24, 14, and finally number 3 by the end of August 1969, where it was behind Johnny Cash's "A Boy Named Sue" and The Rolling Stones' "Honky Tonk Women." "Sugar Sugar" then unseated "Honky Tonk Women" from the number one spot and remained there for a month, famously preventing Creedence Clearwater Revival's "Green River" from reaching number one. This track is described as having a good hook, simple lyrics, and a syncopated rhythm, and is noted for molding the taste of a generation of preteens. "Oh sugar sugar honey you are my candy girl I can't stop wanting you."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
